claim: The hippocampus is critical for memory formation.
source: The hippocampus is critical for memory formation.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in neuroscience supported by extensive research literature.

claim: The hypothalamic supramammillary nucleus (SuM) sends long-range projections to hippocampal area CA2.
source: The hypothalamic supramammillary nucleus (SuM) sends long-range projections to hippocampal area CA2.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: The SuM-CA2 connection is critical for social memory.
source: While the SuM-CA2 connection is critical for social memory, how this input acts on the local circuit is unknown.
evidence: This statement references prior research establishing the importance of this connection for social memory.

claim: SuM axon stimulation elicited mixed excitatory and inhibitory responses in area CA2 pyramidal neurons (PNs).
source: Using transgenic mice, we found that SuM axon stimulation elicited mixed excitatory and inhibitory responses in area CA2 pyramidal neurons (PNs).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Parvalbumin-expressing basket cells were largely responsible for the feedforward inhibitory drive of SuM over area CA2.
source: Parvalbumin-expressing basket cells were largely responsible for the feedforward inhibitory drive of SuM over area CA2.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by multiple experimental approaches including DREADD silencing, pharmacology, and immunohistochemistry.

claim: Inhibition recruited by the SuM input onto CA2 PNs increased the precision of action potential firing both in conditions of low and high cholinergic tone.
source: Inhibition recruited by the SuM input onto CA2 PNs increased the precision of action potential firing both in conditions of low and high cholinergic tone.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings showing reduced AP jitter with SuM stimulation.

claim: SuM stimulation in area CA2 modulated CA1 activity.
source: Furthermore, SuM stimulation in area CA2 modulated CA1 activity, indicating that synchronized CA2 output drives a pulsed inhibition in area CA1.
evidence: This is supported by both in vivo multi-unit recordings and ex vivo whole-cell recordings.

claim: Synchronized CA2 output drives a pulsed inhibition in area CA1.
source: Furthermore, SuM stimulation in area CA2 modulated CA1 activity, indicating that synchronized CA2 output drives a pulsed inhibition in area CA1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of IPSCs in CA1 PNs following SuM stimulation in CA2.

claim: Area CA2 has been shown to play a significant role in social memory formation.
source: While area CA2 has been shown to play a significant role in several hippocampal processes including social memory formation (Hitti and Siegelbaum, 2014; Stevenson and Caldwell, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Area CA2 plays a role in sharp-wave ripple generation.
source: While area CA2 has been shown to play a significant role in several hippocampal processes including social memory formation (Hitti and Siegelbaum, 2014; Stevenson and Caldwell, 2014) sharp-wave ripple generation (Oliva et al., 2016a)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Area CA2 plays a role in spatial encoding.
source: While area CA2 has been shown to play a significant role in several hippocampal processes including social memory formation (Hitti and Siegelbaum, 2014; Stevenson and Caldwell, 2014) sharp-wave ripple generation (Oliva et al., 2016a) and spatial encoding (Kay et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Neurons in area CA2 have unique molecular expression profiles.
source: There is mounting evidence that generalizations cannot be made from the rich understanding of areas CA1 and CA3, as neurons in area CA2 have been shown to have unique molecular expression profiles (Cembrowski et al., 2016; Lein et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neurons in area CA2 have unique morphology.
source: There is mounting evidence that generalizations cannot be made from the rich understanding of areas CA1 and CA3, as neurons in area CA2 have been shown to have unique molecular expression profiles (Cembrowski et al., 2016; Lein et al., 2004), morphology (Bartesaghi and Ravasi, 1999; Nò, 1934)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neurons in area CA2 have unique cellular properties.
source: There is mounting evidence that generalizations cannot be made from the rich understanding of areas CA1 and CA3, as neurons in area CA2 have been shown to have unique molecular expression profiles (Cembrowski et al., 2016; Lein et al., 2004), morphology (Bartesaghi and Ravasi, 1999; Nò, 1934) and cellular properties (Robert et al., 2020; Srinivas et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CA2 pyramidal neurons do not undergo high-frequency stimulation-induced synaptic plasticity.
source: Notably, and in contrast to area CA1, CA2 pyramidal neurons do not undergo high-frequency stimulation-induced synaptic plasticity (Dasgupta et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The excitability of area CA2 is tightly controlled by a highly plastic network of inhibitory neurons.
source: Rather, the excitability of this region is tightly controlled by a highly plastic network of inhibitory neurons (Leroy et al., 2017; Nasrallah et al., 2015; Piskorowski and Chevaleyre, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: When active, CA2 pyramidal neurons can strongly drive area CA1.
source: When active, CA2 pyramidal neurons (PNs) can strongly drive area CA1 (Chevaleyre and Siegelbaum, 2010; Kohara et al., 2014; Nasrallah et al., 2019), thereby influencing hippocampal output.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CA2 neurons project to area CA3, where they recruit inhibition.
source: Furthermore, CA2 neurons also project to area CA3, where they recruit inhibition (Boehringer et al., 2017; Kohara et al., 2014) and act to control hippocampal excitability.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The hypothalamic supramammillary (SuM) nucleus sends projections to both area CA2 and the dentate gyrus (DG).
source: The hypothalamic supramammillary (SuM) nucleus sends projections to both area CA2 and the dentate gyrus (DG) (Haglund et al., 1984; Vertes, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: SuM projections to hippocampus have been shown in rodents, primates, and humans.
source: These long-range connections have been shown in several species including rodents, primates, and humans (Berger et al., 2001; Haglund et al., 1984; Wyss et al., 1979) where they are present in early hippocampal development.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The SuM has been found to be active during novel environment exposure.
source: The SuM has been found to be active during a wide variety of conditions including novel environment exposure (Ito et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The SuM has been found to be active during reinforcement learning.
source: The SuM has been found to be active during a wide variety of conditions including novel environment exposure (Ito et al., 2009), reinforcement learning (Ikemoto, 2005; Ikemoto et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The SuM has been found to be active during food anticipation.
source: The SuM has been found to be active during a wide variety of conditions including novel environment exposure (Ito et al., 2009), reinforcement learning (Ikemoto, 2005; Ikemoto et al., 2004), food anticipation (Le May et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The SuM has been found to be active during REM sleep and arousal.
source: The SuM has been found to be active during a wide variety of conditions including novel environment exposure (Ito et al., 2009), reinforcement learning (Ikemoto, 2005; Ikemoto et al., 2004), food anticipation (Le May et al., 2019), and during REM sleep and arousal (Pedersen et al., 2017; Renouard et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The SuM is known for participating in hippocampal theta rhythm.
source: This nucleus is also known for participating in hippocampal theta rhythm (Pan and McNaughton, 2002; Pan and McNaughton, 1997)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The SuM regulates spike-timing between hippocampus and the cortex.
source: This nucleus is also known for participating in hippocampal theta rhythm (Pan and McNaughton, 2002; Pan and McNaughton, 1997), possibly by its direct projection to the hippocampus or by modulation of the medial septum (Borhegyi et al., 1998; Vertes and Kocsis, 1997), and regulating spike-timing between hippocampus and the cortex (Ito et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Disruption of SuM neuron activity with pharmacological methods has been reported to disrupt hippocampal memory.
source: Disruption of SuM neuron activity with pharmacological methods (Aranda et al., 2008; Shahidi et al., 2004) or lesions (Aranda et al., 2006) has been reported to disrupt hippocampal memory.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Serotonin depletion of the SuM leads to deficiencies in spatial learning in the Morris water maze.
source: Serotonin depletion of the SuM leads to deficiencies in spatial learning in the Morris water maze, and results in altered hippocampal theta activity (Gutiérrez-Guzmán et al., 2012; Hernández-Pérez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Salient rewarding experiences activate the SuM, as evidenced by cFos expression in monoaminergic SuM neurons by consumption of rewarding food.
source: Salient rewarding experiences also activate the SuM, as evidenced by cFos expression in monoaminergic SuM neurons by consumption of rewarding food (Plaisier et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The rewarding aspects of social aggression involve an excitatory circuit between the hypothalamic ventral premammillary nucleus and the SuM.
source: Furthermore, the rewarding aspects of social aggression have been shown to involve an excitatory circuit between the hypothalamic ventral premammillary nucleus and the SuM (Stagkourakis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: There are two separate populations of cells in the SuM that target either CA2 or the DG.
source: It has recently been shown that there are two separate populations of cells in the SuM that target either CA2 or the DG (Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent research.

claim: In the DG, the SuM terminals release both glutamate and GABA.
source: In the DG, the SuM terminals release both glutamate and GABA (Boulland et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2020; Hashimotodani et al., 2018; Pedersen et al., 2017; Soussi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The SuM-DG projection plays a role in modulating DG activity in response to contextual novelty.
source: The SuM-DG projection has been recently shown to play a role in modulating DG activity in response to contextual novelty (Chen et al., 2020) and spatial memory retrieval (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: Functional studies of the SuM-CA2 projection have found that this connection is entirely glutamatergic.
source: In contrast, functional studies of the SuM-CA2 projection have found that this connection is entirely glutamatergic (Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent research.

claim: The CA2-projecting SuM neurons are active during social novelty exposure.
source: It was recently discovered that the CA2-projecting SuM neurons are active during social novelty exposure, and their selective stimulation prevents expression of a memory of a familiar conspecific (Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent research.

claim: Selective stimulation of CA2-projecting SuM neurons prevents expression of a memory of a familiar conspecific.
source: It was recently discovered that the CA2-projecting SuM neurons are active during social novelty exposure, and their selective stimulation prevents expression of a memory of a familiar conspecific (Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent research.

claim: A subset of SuM neurons were active earlier than CA2 and other hippocampal cells during SWR.
source: Furthermore, recent in vivo recordings from the SuM in anesthetized rats reported that a subset of SuM neurons were active earlier than CA2 and other hippocampal cells during SWR (Vicente et al., 2020), indicating a possible role for the SuM-CA2 projection in shaping area CA2 activity prior to SWR onset.
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent research.

claim: The source of vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (VGluT2)-immunopositive boutons in area CA2 originate from the SuM.
source: It has been shown that the source of vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (VGluT2)-immunopositive boutons in area CA2 originate from the SuM (Halasy et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: CA2-projecting cells express calretinin and are located in the medial SuM.
source: Consistent with recent findings using retrograde AAV vectors (Chen et al., 2020), we observed that CA2-projecting cells express calretinin and are located in the medial SuM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by both citation to recent research and immunohistochemical data shown in the figure.

claim: CA2-projecting SuM cells are located bilaterally, ventral to the fiber bundles that traverse the SuM.
source: These cells were located bilaterally, ventral to the fiber bundles that traverse the SuM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in the figure.

claim: CA2-projecting SuM cells stain for VGluT2.
source: Furthermore, we confirmed that these cells also stain for VGluT2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in the figure.

claim: EYFP-containing SuM axons were found throughout the granule cell layer of the DG and in area CA2.
source: EYFP-containing SuM axons were found throughout the granule cell layer of the DG and in area CA2 (Figure 1B) where they clustered around the pyramidal layer (stratum pyramidale, SP).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in the figure.

claim: The SuM fiber projection area was clearly restricted to area CA2, as defined by expression of the CA2-specific markers PCP4 and RGS14.
source: The SuM fiber projection area was clearly restricted to area CA2, as defined by expression of the CA2-specific markers PCP4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and RGS14 (Figure 1B), and did not spread to neighboring areas CA3 and CA1.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in the figures.

claim: Photostimulation of SuM axons elicited excitatory post-synaptic responses in 63% of PNs located in area CA2.
source: We observed that photostimulation of SuM axons elicited excitatory post-synaptic responses in 63% of PNs (n = 166 of 263 cells) located in area CA2.
evidence: This is a primary finding from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The SuM-PN connectivity was not different between CA2 and CA3 PNs.
source: We found that the SuM-PN connectivity was not different between CA2 and CA3 PNs (Table 2, χ² test for CA2 and CA3 PNs, p=0.572)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: The SuM-PN connectivity was not different between deep and superficial PNs.
source: We found that the SuM-PN connectivity was not different between CA2 and CA3 PNs (Table 2, χ² test for CA2 and CA3 PNs, p=0.572) or between deep and superficial PNs (Table 2, χ² test for deep and superficial PNs, p=0.946).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Light-evoked excitatory post-synaptic potentials (EPSPs) and excitatory post-synaptic currents (EPSCs) recorded at −70 mV were of fairly small amplitude.
source: Light-evoked excitatory post-synaptic potentials (EPSPs) and excitatory post-synaptic currents (EPSCs) recorded at −70 mV were of fairly small amplitude (Figure 1C–D)
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figures.

claim: The amplitude of SuM input-evoked post-synaptic responses was similar regardless of the PN type or somatic location.
source: Light-evoked excitatory post-synaptic potentials (EPSPs) and excitatory post-synaptic currents (EPSCs) recorded at −70 mV were of fairly small amplitude (Figure 1C–D) that were similar regardless of the PN type or somatic location (Table 2, Mann-Whitney U test for CA2 and CA3 PNs, p=0.409; Mann-Whitney U test for deep and superficial PNs, p=0.306).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: All SuM transmission was blocked following application of the sodium channel blocker tetrodotoxin (TTX).
source: We are confident that this transmission is due to action potential-generated vesicle release because all transmission was blocked following application of the sodium channel blocker tetrodotoxin (TTX) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in the figure.

claim: The pure glutamatergic nature of the SuM input was confirmed by the complete block of light-evoked synaptic transmission following the application of the AMPA and NMDA receptors antagonists NBQX and D-APV.
source: The pure glutamatergic nature of the SuM input was confirmed by the complete block of light-evoked synaptic transmission following the application of the AMPA and NMDA receptors antagonists NBQX and D-APV (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C; amplitudes were −16 ± 4.8 pA in control and −1.8 ± 0.3 pA in NBQX and D-APV, n = 6; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.03).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in the figure.

claim: SuM inputs provide long-range glutamatergic excitation to CA2 and CA3 PNs in area CA2.
source: These data confirm that SuM inputs provide long-range glutamatergic excitation to CA2 and CA3 PNs in area CA2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: Blocking inhibitory transmission with the GABAA and GABAB receptor antagonists SR95531 and CGP55845A led to a significant increase of light-evoked PSP amplitude recorded in area CA2 PNs.
source: Interestingly, blocking inhibitory transmission with the GABAA and GABAB receptor antagonists SR95531 and CGP55845A led to a significant increase of light-evoked PSP amplitude recorded in area CA2 PNs (Figure 2A–C; amplitudes of the first response were 0.18 ± 0.05 mV in control and 0.24 ± 0.05 mV in SR95531 and CGP55845A, n = 14; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, p=0.004 for the first PSP, p=0.013 for the second PSP, p<0.001 for the third PSP).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in the figure.

claim: SuM-driven excitation is negatively controlled by feedforward inhibition.
source: Thus, this result demonstrates a negative control of SuM-driven excitation by feedforward inhibition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing increased PSP amplitude when inhibition is blocked.

claim: SuM input stimulation paired with SR input had a net depolarizing effect when CA2 PNs were kept at −70 mV.
source: In summary, we found that when the CA2 PNs were kept at −70 mV, SuM input stimulation paired with SR or SLM input had a net depolarizing effect.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data from paired stimulation experiments.

claim: For SR input stimulation, there was no significant difference between the observed paired SR+SuM amplitude and the calculated linear summated amplitude.
source: For SR input stimulation, we found no significant difference between the observed paired SR+SuM amplitude and the calculated linear summated amplitude (SR alone + SuM alone) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figure.

claim: For the SLM input stimulation, the observed paired amplitude was significantly smaller than the linear summation of the two inputs for the first stimulus.
source: However, for the SLM input stimulation, the observed paired amplitude was significantly smaller than the linear summation of the two inputs (SLM alone + SuM alone) for the first stimulus (n = 10; T test, p=0.014) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figure.

claim: There was a significant reduction of the summation ratio for both SR and SLM inputs when paired with SuM stimulation.
source: We observed a significant reduction of the summation ratio as measured by the ratio of the n-th pulse to the first (Pn/P1) for both SR (n = 10; repeated-measures ANOVA, p=2.3×10−4) and SLM (n = 10; repeated-measures ANOVA, p=8.5×10−4).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Concomitant SuM activity reduces the level of facilitation of several pulses in a train, preventing cellular excitation from other inputs.
source: This observation that concomitant SuM activity is reducing the level of facilitation of several pulses in a train indicates that the short-term dynamics of the SuM-driven excitation and feedforward inhibition are playing a role to prevent cellular excitation from other inputs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on summation ratios.

claim: Robust light-evoked excitatory transmission from SuM axons was observed in 35 out of 62 interneurons with soma located in SP.
source: In contrast with previous reports of an exclusive innervation of PNs by SuM (Maglóczky et al., 1994), we observed robust light-evoked excitatory transmission from SuM axons in 35 out of 62 interneurons (INs) with soma located in SP.
evidence: This is a primary finding from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: 22 cells were classified as basket cells (BCs) because their axonal arborizations were restricted to SP.
source: We classified 22 cells as basket cells (BCs) because their axonal arborizations were restricted to SP (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis of recorded cells shown in the figure.

claim: Light-evoked EPSCs and PSPs were readily observed in the vast majority of BCs.
source: Light-evoked EPSCs and PSPs were readily observed in the vast majority of BCs (Figure 3A, C and D, Table 4) and reached large amplitudes in some instances.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figures and table.

claim: 26 INs with soma in SP were classified as non-BCs because their axon did not target SP.
source: An additional 26 INs with soma in SP were classified as non-BCs because their axon did not target SP (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis of recorded cells shown in the figure.

claim: No or very minor light-evoked excitatory transmission was consistently observed onto non-BCs.
source: We consistently observed no or very minor light-evoked excitatory transmission onto non-BCs (Figure 3B–C, Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figures and table.

claim: SuM input preferentially forms excitatory synapses onto basket cells in area CA2.
source: This data is consistent with the conclusion that SuM input preferentially forms excitatory synapses onto basket cells in area CA2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing stronger connectivity and responses in BCs compared to other cell types.

claim: BCs could fire action potentials upon SuM input photostimulation leading to a substantial feedforward inhibition of neighboring PNs.
source: These BCs could fire action potentials upon SuM input photostimulation leading to a substantial feedforward inhibition of neighboring PNs.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing AP firing in BCs and IPSCs in PNs.

claim: At resting membrane potentials, the mixed excitatory/inhibitory SuM input resulted in a net depolarization of the membrane potential in CA2 PNs.
source: We found that at resting membrane potentials, the mixed excitatory/inhibitory SuM input resulted in a net depolarization of the membrane potential in CA2 PNs.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings at resting membrane potential.

claim: When the SuM input was paired with either inputs in SR or SLM, there was a decrease in the summation ratios of trains of synaptic inputs consistent with a perisomatic shunting inhibition driven by SuM in area CA2.
source: However, when the SuM input was paired with either inputs in SR or SLM, we observed a decrease in the summation ratios of trains of synaptic inputs consistent with a perisomatic shunting inhibition driven by SuM in area CA2.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data from paired stimulation experiments.

claim: With elevated cholinergic tone, recruitment of BCs by SuM controlled PNs excitability and shaped spontaneous burst firing.
source: Furthermore, we found that with elevated cholinergic tone, recruitment of BCs by SuM controlled PNs excitability and shaped spontaneous burst firing.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in the presence of carbachol.

claim: SuM activity can pace action potential firing in PNs through recruitment of feedforward inhibition.
source: This finding demonstrates that SuM activity can pace action potential firing in PNs through recruitment of feedforward inhibition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing reduced AP jitter with SuM stimulation.

claim: The population of INs potently excited by SuM transmission display many features that classify them as PV+ BCs.
source: The population of INs potently excited by SuM transmission display many features that motivate us to classify them as PV+ BCs.
evidence: This is based on multiple lines of evidence including morphology, electrophysiology, and immunohistochemistry.

claim: PV-immunoreactivity could unequivocally be detected in either the soma or dendrites of seven connected BCs.
source: However, PV-immunoreactivity could unequivocally be detected in either the soma or dendrites of seven connected BCs (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in the figure.

claim: At least a fraction of the recorded BCs connected by the SuM is expressing PV.
source: Therefore, this data demonstrates that at least a fraction of the recorded BCs connected by the SuM is expressing PV.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunohistochemical data.

claim: The selective expression of GiDREADD in PV+ cells allows for selective silencing that reduces SuM-driven feedforward inhibition of area CA2 PNs.
source: The selective expression of GiDREADD in PV+ cells allows for selective silencing that reduces SuM-driven feedforward inhibition of area CA2 PNs.
evidence: This is supported by DREADD experiments showing reduced IPSCs with CNO application.

claim: A substantial reduction of SuM-evoked IPSC amplitude was observed in area CA2 PNs upon application of 10 µM of the Gi-DREADD ligand CNO.
source: We observed a substantial reduction of SuM-evoked IPSC amplitude recorded in area CA2 PNs upon application of 10 µM of the Gi-DREADD ligand CNO (Figure 5C; amplitudes were 847 ± 122 pA in control and 498 ± 87 pA in CNO hence a 42 ± 6.0% block, n = 13; paired-T test, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacogenetic data shown in the figure.

claim: PV+ cells are predominantly targeted by SuM inputs in area CA2.
source: Altogether, these four methods strongly suggest that SuM inputs selectively recruit PV +interneurons to inhibit CA2 PNs. Although individually each method does not conclusively demonstrate that SuM input exclusively targets PV+ INs, the consistent reduction of SuM-driven feedforward inhibition of CA2 PNs observed with every approach allows us to conclude that PV + cells are predominantly targeted by SuM inputs in area CA2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The feedforward inhibitory transmission recruited by SuM stimulation is highly sensitive to MOR activation.
source: The feedforward inhibitory transmission recruited by SuM stimulation is highly sensitive to MOR activation.
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data showing near complete block of IPSCs with DAMGO.

claim: There was a near complete block of the light-evoked IPSC amplitude following 1 μM DAMGO application.
source: We found that there was a near complete block of the light-evoked IPSC amplitude following 1 μM DAMGO application (Figure 5E 1; IPSC amplitudes were 343 ± 123 pA in control and 31 ± 12.4 pA in DAMGO hence a 88 ± 5.0% block, n = 6 PNs; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.031)
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in the figure.

claim: Direct excitatory transmission remained unaffected by DAMGO application.
source: while direct excitatory transmission remained unaffected (Figure 5E 2; EPSC amplitudes were −6.7 ± 1.1 pA in SR95531 and CGP55845A and −5.6 ± 0.9 pA after DAMGO, n = 17 PNs; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.19).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in the figure.

claim: The SuM-recruited feedforward inhibition is sensitive to DOR activation.
source: We also show that the SuM-recruited feedforward inhibition is sensitive to DOR activation.
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data showing reduction of IPSCs with DPDPE.

claim: Application of 0.5 µM of the DOR agonist DPDPE led to a long-term reduction of light-evoked IPSCs recorded in area CA2 PNs.
source: Application of 0.5 µM of the DOR agonist DPDPE led to a long-term reduction of light-evoked IPSCs recorded in area CA2 PNs, similar to the iLTD seen by CA3 input stimulation (Figure 5F 1; IPSC amplitudes were 168 ± 28 pA in control and 64 ± 22 pA in DPDPE hence a 61 ± 14% block by DPDPE, n = 7; paired-T test, p=0.015)
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in the figure.

claim: Both the local CA3 and long-range SuM inputs converge onto an overlapping population of INs to inhibit area CA2 PNs.
source: Further confirming the PV+ nature of INs responsible for the SuM feedforward inhibition, this result reveals that both the local CA3 and long-range SuM inputs converge onto an overlapping population of INs to inhibit area CA2 PNs, thus enabling cross-talk between these routes through synaptic plasticity of PV+ INs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DOR sensitivity data.

claim: Recruitment of SuM inputs significantly delayed the onset of the first AP in CA2 PNs.
source: We observed that recruitment of SuM inputs significantly delayed the onset of the first AP (Figure 6C; latency to the first AP were 221 ± 19.9 ms in control and 233 ± 19.1 ms with photostimulation, hence a 12.1 ± 4.3 ms increase upon photostimulation, n = 12; paired-T test, p=0.016).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figure.

claim: Photostimulation of SuM axons at 10 Hz led to a significant decrease of variability in the timing of AP firing by PNs.
source: Indeed, photostimulation of SuM axons at 10 Hz led to a significant decrease of variability in the timing of AP firing by PNs (Figure 6D–E; standard deviations of the first AP timing were 36.9 ± 11 ms in control and 24.7 ± 7.4 ms with photostimulation, hence a 12.3 ± 5.3 ms decrease upon photostimulation, n = 12; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, p<0.001 for the first AP, p=0.008 for the second AP, p=0.004 for the third AP).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figure.

claim: Both the delay of AP onset and the reduction of AP jitter stemmed from the feedforward inhibition recruited by SuM inputs.
source: Both the delay of AP onset and the reduction of AP jitter stemmed from the feedforward inhibition recruited by SuM inputs as application of GABAA and GABAB receptor antagonists abolished these effects of SuM stimulation (Figure 6C–E; latency to the first AP were 232 ± 19.8 ms in SR95531 and CGP55845A and 235 ± 18.0 ms with photostimulation, n = 6; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.44; standard deviations of the first AP timing were 11.9 ± 2.0 ms in SR95531 and CGP55845A and 7.1 ± 1.5 ms with photostimulation, n = 6; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, p=0.22 for the first AP, p=0.16 for the second AP, p=0.09 for the third AP).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in the figure.

claim: The purely glutamatergic SuM input, by recruiting feedforward inhibition, has an overall inhibitory effect on PN excitability.
source: These results reveal that the purely glutamatergic SuM input, by recruiting feedforward inhibition, has an overall inhibitory effect on PN excitability and can influence the timing and jitter of area CA2 PN action potential firing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing delayed and more precise AP firing with SuM stimulation.

claim: The AP discharge of SuM neurons in vivo is phase-locked to the hippocampal theta rhythm.
source: It has been reported that the AP discharge of SuM neurons in vivo is phase-locked to the hippocampal theta rhythm (Kocsis and Vertes, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: CCh decreased the amplitude and increased the PPR of SuM-evoked EPSCs in CA2 PNs.
source: With GABA receptors blocked to first assess the SuM excitatory transmission only, we observed that CCh decreased the amplitude and increased the PPR of SuM-evoked EPSCs in CA2 PNs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in the figure.

claim: CCh application decreased IPSC amplitude and increased PPR for SuM-evoked feedforward inhibitory transmission to CA2 PNs.
source: We found similar results for SuM-evoked feedforward inhibitory transmission to CA2 PNs as IPSC amplitude was decreased and PPR increased with CCh application (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in the figure.

claim: Both SuM-evoked EPSCs and IPSCs underwent short-term depression.
source: We observed that both SuM-evoked EPSCs and IPSCs underwent short-term depression, as evidenced by a decrease in amplitude along the pulse train as well as amplitude ratios between subsequent pulses over the first pulse (Pn/P1) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figure.

claim: The E/I ratio did not significantly change with repeated SuM input stimulation.
source: It is worth noting that the Pn/P1 ratio was similar for EPSCs and IPSCs and that the E/I ratio did not significantly change with repeated SuM input stimulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F–G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figure.

claim: The SuM influence over CA2 PN may remain overall inhibitory during prolonged SuM input activation.
source: This indicates that the SuM influence over CA2 PN may remain overall inhibitory during prolonged SuM input activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the E/I ratio does not change significantly with repeated stimulation.

claim: Application of 10 µM CCh decreased the amplitude of the initial response of SuM-evoked PSCs.
source: Similarly influencing both EPSCs and IPSCs, application of 10 µM CCh affected these short-term dynamics of the SuM-CA2 PN transmission by decreasing the amplitude of the initial response (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1—source data 1)
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in the figure.

claim: CCh application limited the subsequent short-term depression of SuM-evoked PSCs amplitude.
source: Similarly influencing both EPSCs and IPSCs, application of 10 µM CCh affected these short-term dynamics of the SuM-CA2 PN transmission by decreasing the amplitude of the initial response (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1—source data 1) but limiting the subsequent short-term depression of SuM-evoked PSCs amplitude (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in the figure.

claim: The E/I ratio of PSCs during the pulse train was lower in CCh as compared to control.
source: Interestingly, the overall effect of repeated SuM input stimulation on post-synaptic responses in area CA2 PNs was even more biased toward inhibition after CCh application as the E/I ratio of PSCs during the pulse train was lower in CCh as compared to control (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1—source data 1)
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figure.

claim: There was a significant decrease in the number of APs fired during a burst when SuM inputs were photostimulated as compared to interleaved control bursts.
source: We observed a significant decrease in the number of APs fired during a burst when SuM inputs were photostimulated as compared to interleaved control bursts (Figure 7C–D; numbers of APs per burst were 15.2 ± 2.3 in control and 6.9 ± 1.3 with photostimulation, n = 7; paired-T test, p=0.031).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figure.

claim: In the photostimulation bursts, the initial increase of AP firing frequency was absent, and the subsequent AP firing frequency was reduced.
source: In control bursts, the AP firing rate of CA2 PNs initially increases, and then progressively decreases. In the photostimulation bursts, the initial increase of AP firing frequency was absent, and the subsequent AP firing frequency was reduced (Figure 7E; two-way ANOVA on firing rate over time in light-on vs light-off conditions; light factor, p<0.001; time factor, p<0.001; light x time factor, p=0.052).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figure.

claim: Photostimulation of SuM inputs resulted in a striking reduction in the amount of time the membrane potential remained depolarized.
source: We observed that photostimulation of SuM inputs resulted in a striking reduction in the amount of time the membrane potential remained depolarized, and this is likely why the burst duration was significantly shorter in bursts with SuM photo-stimulation (Figure 7F–G; burst duration was 4.0 ± 1.1 s in control and 1.6 ± 0.5 s with photostimulation, n = 7; paired-T test, p=0.037).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figure.

claim: AP bursts with SuM input activation were followed more rapidly by another burst of APs than the ones without SuM input activation.
source: Indeed, AP bursts with SuM input activation were followed more rapidly by another burst of APs than the ones without SuM input activation (Figure 7B and H; time until next burst was 93 ± 14 s in control and 59 ± 17 s with photostimulation, n = 7; paired-T test, p=0.001)
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figure.

claim: SuM input activation is able to modify the spontaneous bursting activity of CA2 PNs under conditions of high cholinergic tone.
source: Thus, in our preparation, SuM input activation is able to modify the spontaneous bursting activity of CA2 PNs under conditions of high cholinergic tone.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing altered burst properties with SuM stimulation in the presence of carbachol.

claim: The activation of SuM terminals in CA2 resulted in a significant and reproducible change in the multiunit spiking activity recorded in the pyramidal cell layer of CA1 on 34 of 55 tetrodes.
source: Across 23 recording sessions in five mice, we found that the activation of SuM terminals in CA2 resulted in a significant and reproducible change in the multiunit spiking activity recorded in the pyramidal cell layer of CA1 on 34 of 55 tetrodes.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo multi-unit recording data.

claim: The firing rate change in CA1 showed a decrease starting shortly after laser onset and continuing for about 10 ms, followed immediately by a rebound-like increase to about 20% greater than baseline firing rate.
source: The firing rate change was similar across individual tetrodes (Figure 8B–C), with a decrease in the normalized firing rate starting shortly after laser onset and continuing for about 10 ms, followed immediately by a rebound-like increase to about 20% greater than baseline firing rate (Figure 8B–C).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo multi-unit recording data shown in the figure.

claim: Whole-cell recordings of CA1 PNs showed an absence of EPSCs time-locked to the photostimulation in all but one case.
source: Whole-cell recordings of CA1 PNs showed an absence of EPSCs time-locked to the photostimulation in all but one case (n = 11/12) (Figure 8E–F).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo electrophysiological data shown in the figure.

claim: Light-evoked IPSCs in CA1 PNs were often observed occurring 10–20 ms after light onset.
source: In contrast, we often (n = 7/12) observed light-evoked IPSCs in CA1 PNs occurring 10–20 ms after light onset (Figure 8G–H).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo electrophysiological data shown in the figure.

claim: The reduction in firing of CA1 units in vivo is likely caused by increased inhibitory inputs onto CA1 PNs within 10–20 ms of SuM fiber stimulation over area CA2.
source: Therefore, the reduction in firing of CA1 units in vivo is likely caused by increased inhibitory inputs onto CA1 PNs within 10–20 ms of SuM fiber stimulation over area CA2.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of IPSCs in CA1 PNs ex vivo and decreased firing in vivo with similar timing.

claim: SuM input contributes to controlling CA2 output that regulates CA1 activity in vivo.
source: This result highlights a contribution of SuM input to controlling CA2 output that regulate CA1 activity in vivo and provides a mechanistic interpretation of this observation at the circuit level.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined in vivo and ex vivo data.

claim: SuM input forms synapses onto both PNs and INs in area CA2.
source: We found that, in contrast to previous anatomical reports, SuM input forms synapses onto both PNs and INs in area CA2.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The excitatory drive evoked by light-stimulation of SuM input was significantly larger for BC INs.
source: The excitatory drive evoked by light-stimulation of SuM input was significantly larger for BC INs, which we demonstrate are likely PV+.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological and immunohistochemical data.

claim: The resulting feedforward inhibition recruited by SuM input stimulation enhanced the precision of AP timing of CA2 PNs in conditions of low and high cholinergic tone relevant to different brain states.
source: The resulting feedforward inhibition recruited by SuM input stimulation enhanced the precision of AP timing of CA2 PNs in conditions of low and high cholinergic tone relevant to different brain states.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data showing reduced AP jitter with SuM stimulation.

claim: The modified CA2 output evoked poly-synaptic inhibition in area CA1, likely responsible for a decrease in firing rate of CA1 units in vivo.
source: The modified CA2 output evoked poly-synaptic inhibition in area CA1, likely responsible for a decrease in firing rate of CA1 units in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by both in vivo and ex vivo data showing decreased CA1 firing and increased IPSCs.

claim: SuM input controls CA2 output to area CA1 by recruiting feedforward inhibition.
source: Overall, we demonstrate that SuM input controls CA2 output to area CA1 by recruiting feedforward inhibition.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Both intra-hippocampal inputs from CA3 and long-range inputs from the SuM converge onto PV +INs to control CA2 PN excitability and output.
source: Hence, both intra-hippocampal inputs from CA3 and long-range inputs from the SuM converge onto PV +INs to control CA2 PN excitability and output.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that both inputs recruit PV+ INs.

claim: Postmortem studies have reported losses of PV +INs in area CA2 in pathological contexts including bipolar disorder.
source: Postmortem studies have reported losses of PV +INs in area CA2 in pathological contexts including bipolar disorder (Benes et al., 1998)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Postmortem studies have reported losses of PV +INs in area CA2 in Alzheimer's disease.
source: Postmortem studies have reported losses of PV +INs in area CA2 in pathological contexts including bipolar disorder (Benes et al., 1998), Alzheimer's disease (Brady and Mufson, 1997)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Postmortem studies have reported losses of PV +INs in area CA2 in schizophrenia.
source: Postmortem studies have reported losses of PV +INs in area CA2 in pathological contexts including bipolar disorder (Benes et al., 1998), Alzheimer's disease (Brady and Mufson, 1997), and schizophrenia (Benes et al., 1998; Knable et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In a mouse model of the 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, there was a loss of PV staining and deficit of inhibitory transmission in area CA2 that were accompanied by impairments in social memory.
source: Consistent with these reports, in a mouse model of the 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, a major risk factor for schizophrenia in humans, we found a loss of PV staining and deficit of inhibitory transmission in area CA2 that were accompanied by impairments in social memory (Piskorowski et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The DOR-mediated plasticity onto PV +INs is altered in the 22q11.2 deletion syndrome mouse model.
source: Indeed, the DOR-mediated plasticity onto PV +INs is altered in the 22q11.2 deletion syndrome mouse model, and we show here that a fraction of the PV +INs targeted by the SuM also express DOR.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research and data from the current study.

claim: A fraction of the PV +INs targeted by the SuM also express DOR.
source: Indeed, the DOR-mediated plasticity onto PV +INs is altered in the 22q11.2 deletion syndrome mouse model, and we show here that a fraction of the PV +INs targeted by the SuM also express DOR.
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data showing DOR sensitivity of SuM-evoked inhibition.

claim: The loss of function of PV +INs in area CA2 could disrupt proper long-range connection between the hippocampus and the hypothalamus.
source: Thus, the loss of function of PV +INs in area CA2 could disrupt proper long-range connection between the hippocampus and the hypothalamus and possibly contribute to some of the cognitive impairments observed in schizophrenic patients and animal models.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the findings of the study and previous research.

claim: Pharmacological mouse models of schizophrenia have reported increased c-fos immunoreactivity in the SuM as well as memory impairments.
source: Further, pharmacological mouse models of schizophrenia have reported increased c-fos immunoreactivity in the SuM as well as memory impairments (Castañé et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Abnormalities of the SuM projection onto area CA2 appear as a potential mechanism that warrants further investigation in schizophrenia models.
source: Although several alterations in these models of schizophrenia could lead to deficits of hippocampal-dependent behavior, abnormalities of the SuM projection onto area CA2 appear as a potential mechanism that warrants further investigation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement suggesting future research directions.
